title: Void Rift - A Claude Code gamedev retrospective and a demo
author: VortiK_0683
selftext:
Playable Link: [https://voidrifter84.itch.io/void-rift](https://voidrifter84.itch.io/void-rift)

Since February I've been building Void Rift, a 2D co-op space shooter almost entirely with Claude Code, on evenings and weekends, next to a full-time job and a family.

It runs with Phaser 3 and TypeScript directly in browser and support gamepads up to 4 players local or online. I wanted something easy to pickup but still with some tactical depth. My kids are the main playtesters and feature requesters.

I'm a backend web developer, so I have some knowledge in code and architecture but can't do any art or sound.

A Free demo is now out on itch [https://voidrifter84.itch.io/void-rift](https://voidrifter84.itch.io/void-rift) and I wanted to share a retrospective on the experience.

**The numbers**

* \~7 months, \~790 h over 270 sessions (from git history, so approximative)
* \~4,860 commits, \~115k lines of TypeScript
* \~$900 total, on a Claude Team subscription

**What worked**

* **Fast iteration on a playable work in progress.** Even during big refactors, every change kept a playable build.
* **A skills workflow made organically.** It ended on the classic *idea* \> *spec* \> *implement* \> *test*, plus a few domain "experts" skills (UI, game design, sound). One of the first skills was */coach*, which reviews sessions and points out friction. A */skill-craft* skill then builds and maintains the rest. Claude improving your Claude usage!
* **Context management.** A compact [CLAUDE.md](http://CLAUDE.md), domain memory files, design docs with a progress section make sure nothing is forgotten. I can pick up a feature anytime or take a break when needed.
* **TypeScript and tests.** It started in plain javascript, that I don't even know to code myself and invested in a Typescript migration that took a long week. It was very worth it as with the LSP plugin Claude catches breaking changes before the tests even run, and it also keeps lint and tests green on its own.

**What hurt**

* **Subagents** burn the token limits and it took a long time to finetune when to delegate properly and efficiently.
* **Picking models.** I settled on a design with a strong model and implement with Opus or Sonnet, this is now a "relative tiers" rule. Fable for design and prototypes, Opus for most of the coding and Sonnet for small tasks. And we don't talk about poor Haiku. Nowadays Opus 5.5 just does everything better and much cheaper than Fable.
* **"The code is correct" bugs.** Tests can be green, but the play isn't right. I have to check and and test the game often to judge. Also Claude uses the Chrome MCP a lot to check at runtime, he can't use a gamepad but that helps.
* **Guessing at performance.** Measuring before optimising beats guessing. 90% of the time the cause was not what me or Claude assumed.
* **Autopilot and multitasking.** When tired I ended accepting every "recommended" choice and it just produced slop. Running 2–4 sessions in parallel not only burns through tokens it also overload your brain quickly.
* **80/20 is alive and well.** Claude codes fast, but polishing, judging and reworking still take most of the time.

**Burnout and Fable**

In June I burned out on a procedural planet generator that kept growing, and I didn't touch the project for a month. After some cooldown I rescoped, I needed backgrounds, not a NASA simulation.  
Then Fable arrived and of course I used it to see what it could do, it "one-shotted" impressive stuff but at one point half my time went into refactoring.  
This lead to a proper "think of the architecture" step before coding, data owner, sim vs render, network serialization. Claude will build you a plane if you ask it, but you still just need to go to the grocery store.

**Art and sound**

Claude isn't the best artist LLM but it's still far better than me and it can see pixel so screnshots help it a lot. The simple neon/vector style is the compromise to not spend tons of time on art.  
Sound however is much harder and while Claude can measure audio it just can't hear it. The space/sci-fi theme doesn't help as free good sound packs are rare and looking for sound take a lot of time.  
If you have an AI-assisted audio workflow that works, I'd love to hear about it.

**Conclusion**

As almost anyone can now make a game as seen on the tons of impressive "one-prompts" and while it still takes tons of time and effort to finish and polish a proper game, the real resource is the limited public attention.  
Hence this post to try to share the experience and see if there some interest in what I built. If you made it this far, I'd be very happy to get your feedback on the demo!

There's a more detailed post on the itch blog, I wanted to keep this post shorter and a too big of a wall of text [https://voidrifter84.itch.io/void-rift/devlog/1687578/zero-art-skills-zero-audio-skills-a-day-job-and-kids-my-claude-code-gamedev-retrospective](https://voidrifter84.itch.io/void-rift/devlog/1687578/zero-art-skills-zero-audio-skills-a-day-job-and-kids-my-claude-code-gamedev-retrospective)
